senses.label: Couriers, letters and fire signals
senses.summary: Messages travel at the speed of a rider or ship; beacons and torch codes carry a few prearranged signals faster.
markers: news arrives days or weeks after the event
a message is a physical object carried by a person
hazards: The imperial post moved officials and dispatches, not private conversation.

sources.note: Fire signalling and its limits, including a torch alphabet.
Augustus establishes relays of couriers and vehicles: the imperial post.

senses.label: Optical telegraph
senses.summary: Chains of semaphore towers relay coded messages across a country in minutes.
markers: a message crosses a country in minutes without a carrier

senses.label: Electric telegraph
senses.summary: Coded electrical pulses along wires carry messages almost instantly between distant offices.
markers: messages travel along wires at near-instant speed

sources.citation: Cooke and Wheatstone patent, 1837; Morse line Washington–Baltimore, 1844

senses.label: Telephone
senses.summary: The voice itself is carried live over wires between two people.
markers: two people converse live across great distances

senses.label: Video call
senses.summary: People see and hear each other live across a distance.
markers: people see and hear each other live across a distance

sources.citation: Bell System Picturephone, New York World's Fair (April 1964)
sources.note: Public demonstration of two-way video calling; commercial service followed that year.

senses.label: The internet
senses.summary: Computers in distant places are linked in one network, and work, friendship and meeting are carried on through it.
markers: work, friendship and meeting happen through a network of computers
hazards: Bare 'platform' (railway, political; Darwin uses it 4 times) and bare 'digital' (anatomical digits) are old words: only the phrases are terms.

sources.note: First host-to-host message over the ARPANET, the precursor of the internet.

senses.label: Email
senses.summary: Written messages arrive instantly over computer networks and wait in an inbox.
markers: written messages arrive instantly and pile up waiting to be read

sources.citation: Ray Tomlinson, network email on ARPANET, 1971

senses.label: Mobile phone
senses.summary: A pocket device connects by radio to a network from almost anywhere, for calls and short text messages.
markers: anyone can be reached anywhere, at any hour
messages arrive instantly wherever the person is

sources.citation: Motorola handheld call, 1973; commercial cellular service from 1983

senses.label: Smartphone
senses.summary: A networked pocket computer that delivers news, messages and feeds continuously and signals for attention.
markers: a device constantly signals for its owner's attention
endless content is designed to keep the user looking
alerts from a device interrupt its owner throughout the day
messages are checked on a screen many times a day
hazards: 'Checking' a device is a modern habit with no ancient equivalent; letters were not constant.

sources.note: Earlier devices existed (1994); 2007 marks mass adoption.
